identity.title: Food Safety Plan for Ready-to-Eat Hummus and Bean Dips

scan.summary: This is a food safety plan prepared under 21 CFR Part 117 (FSMA Preventive Controls) for refrigerated ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips made at Willamette Valley Foods' Salem plant. The plan describes the hazard analysis, preventive controls, monitoring procedures, corrective actions, and verification activities required to ensure the safety of products with a 45-day refrigerated shelf life distributed in Oregon, Washington, and Idaho.
scan.freshness_note: This plan became effective May 12, 2025, making it about 16 months old as of September 2026. The plan should be reviewed annually or whenever significant changes occur; request a current version if any production changes have been made since May 2025.

gaps.title: Allergen control for tahini receipt not fully detailed
gaps.description: The plan does not describe how the company verifies that tahini suppliers have allergen controls in place. Section 8 requires third-party audit certificates and certificates of analysis, but does not specify what those audits must cover or how the company verifies the supplier controls are adequate for sesame allergen hazards.
gaps.fix: Add to section 8 a description of what the third-party audit must verify regarding sesame allergen controls at the supplier, including cross-contamination prevention, labeling verification, and any other controls relevant to sesame hazard prevention. Document how the company reviews these audit findings.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 121.126 requires allergen controls to include verification of supplier controls
gaps.quote: Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot.

gaps.title: No direct supplier audit or testing requirement specified
gaps.description: The plan requires suppliers to provide third-party audit certificates but does not specify that the company itself must review those certificates for adequacy or conduct any direct verification (such as on-site audits, testing, or review of supplier's food safety documentation). The rule requires verification that suppliers have controls, which typically includes reviewing evidence of those controls.
gaps.fix: Add to section 8 a statement that the quality manager will review the third-party audit certificate to verify it includes assessment of food safety controls relevant to the product's hazards, particularly allergen and pathogen controls. Consider specifying a frequency for this review (e.g., prior to approval and annually thereafter) and document this review.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 121.126(a) requires allergen controls to include verification that suppliers have controls in place; 21 CFR 121.86 addresses supplier verification generally
gaps.quote: Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot.

gaps.title: Listeria environmental monitoring frequency may be insufficient
gaps.description: The plan specifies weekly environmental monitoring swabs (10 sites, zone 1 and 2) for Listeria spp. and monthly finished product testing. However, for a ready-to-eat product with a 45-day shelf life and post-process exposure to the environment, the rule requires verification activities to ensure controls are working. The plan does not explain why weekly monitoring is adequate or describe a trend analysis that would identify emerging patterns before product safety is compromised.
gaps.fix: Review the adequacy of weekly monitoring frequency based on the product's shelf life (45 days) and risk of Listeria growth during storage. Consider whether more frequent monitoring (e.g., multiple times per week) is needed for certain high-risk zones. Document the justification for the chosen frequency in the plan. Ensure section 7 describes how environmental results are trended and what triggers an increase in monitoring frequency.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 121.149(f) requires the food safety plan to include verification activities; 21 CFR 121.150(a) requires environmental monitoring for pathogens in RTE products
gaps.locator: section 4, Preventive controls (Listeria sanitation control); section 7, Verification
gaps.quote: environmental monitoring swabs weekly... Environmental monitoring results are trended quarterly

gaps.title: No written procedure for PCQI review timeline
gaps.description: Section 6 states corrective actions are reviewed by the PCQI within seven days, and section 7 states records are reviewed within seven working days, but the plan does not describe whether there is a written procedure documenting when and how the PCQI conducts this review, who is responsible if the PCQI is unavailable, or what happens if corrective action records are not reviewed within the timeline.
gaps.fix: Add a written procedure to section 6 or 7 describing: (1) the specific day and time the PCQI conducts the weekly review; (2) the process for coverage if the PCQI is unavailable; (3) how the review is documented (e.g., signature and date on the corrective action log); (4) what escalation occurs if a review deadline is missed. This procedure should reference the seven-day requirement and explain how it is enforced.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 121.160 requires the plan to describe corrective actions and verification
gaps.quote: All corrective actions are recorded on the corrective action log and reviewed by the PCQI within seven days.

gaps.title: Blast chiller temperature monitoring may miss early-phase cooling
gaps.description: The cooling control in section 4 requires cooling from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours and then 70°F to 41°F within 4 hours. However, section 5 states the operator records temperature only at 2 hours and at 6 hours. This means there is no monitoring of the critical early phase (0 to 2 hours), which is when pathogens like Clostridium perfringens and Bacillus cereus spores are most likely to germinate and grow if temperature control fails.
gaps.fix: Modify section 5 to require temperature recording at time zero (immediately after cook), at 1 hour, at 2 hours, and at 6 hours. Alternatively, if the blast chiller has continuous temperature data logging, specify that the log is reviewed to verify compliance with the 135°F to 70°F in 2 hours limit. Ensure monitoring covers the entire cooling period to detect deviations early.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 121.135(a) requires monitoring procedures that ensure critical limits are met during production; 21 CFR 121.140 requires preventive measures for biological hazards
gaps.quote: The blast chiller operator records the temperature at 2 hours and at 6 hours on the cooling log.

gaps.title: Recall plan not described
gaps.description: The plan does not include a written recall procedure. Section 9 mentions records are available to FDA and Oregon Department of Agriculture, but there is no procedure for how the company would identify affected product, notify distributors and consumers, retrieve product, or determine root cause in the event of a food safety incident.
gaps.fix: Add a section 11 (Recall Plan) that describes: (1) how the company will identify affected product lots based on dates and line information; (2) the notification process for distributors, retailers, and consumers; (3) procedures for product retrieval and destruction; (4) how effectiveness of the recall will be verified; (5) roles and responsibilities (e.g., who initiates, who notifies FDA); (6) a template notification letter. This section should reference the product tracking system described in section 5 and available in sections 1 and 4.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 121.160(a) requires the food safety plan to include a recall plan

gaps.title: No description of corrective action effectiveness testing
gaps.description: Section 6 describes corrective actions (e.g., re-cooking a batch, re-cleaning a surface, re-running product through the metal detector) but does not explain how the company verifies that the corrective action actually rendered the product safe or eliminated the hazard. For example, if cooling time is exceeded and a batch is discarded, the plan does not state whether the company tests that batch for pathogens before disposal, nor does it explain how the company verifies the blast chiller is working correctly after a failure.
gaps.fix: Add to section 6 a description of effectiveness testing for each corrective action. For example: (1) if a cook batch is re-cooked, verify the new internal temperature; (2) if a Listeria swab is positive, re-swab and document a negative result before releasing product; (3) if cooling exceeds limits, discard the batch (as stated) but also describe any testing done before discard; (4) if metal detector fails, visually inspect product before reprocessing; (5) add annual or after-incident equipment validation testing (e.g., CCP calibration). This section should be cross-referenced with section 7 (Verification).
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 121.140(a) requires corrective actions to be effective in ensuring the food is safe
gaps.quote: If a cook batch does not reach 212°F for 60 minutes, the batch is re-cooked to the critical limit or discarded, and the cause is recorded.

gaps.title: Definition of 'approved suppliers' not in the plan
gaps.description: Section 8 refers to 'approved suppliers' but does not define what makes a supplier 'approved' beyond requiring a third-party audit certificate and certificate of analysis. The plan does not specify: what certifications are acceptable, how often suppliers must be re-evaluated, what happens if an audit is expired, or criteria for removing a supplier from the approved list.
gaps.fix: Add to section 8 a clear definition of an 'approved supplier,' including: (1) minimum audit standards (e.g., SQF, BRC, FSSC 22000, or equivalent); (2) maximum age of audit certificate (e.g., no older than 2 years); (3) acceptable scope of audit (must include food safety controls relevant to the ingredients supplied); (4) re-approval frequency; (5) criteria for suspension or removal (e.g., audit failure, failed certificate of analysis, recall); (6) reference to the approved supplier list maintained by the quality manager, including date last reviewed.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 121.86 requires supplier verification that includes review of food safety audit results
gaps.quote: Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot.

scan.confidence_notes: High confidence in the identification and structure of this document. It is clearly a food safety plan for FSMA Preventive Controls (21 CFR Part 117). The gaps identified are based on direct comparison to 21 CFR 121 requirements and are well-grounded in regulatory language. The three most significant gaps are: (1) the recall plan is completely absent, which is a mandatory element; (2) supplier verification lacks specificity about what constitutes an 'approved' supplier and lacks procedures for reviewing audit adequacy; (3) early-phase cooling temperature monitoring is missing, creating a monitoring gap during the period of highest risk for spore-former growth. I am confident in these findings. Medium confidence in whether the PCQI certification is still current—the document states Dana Whitfield completed FSPCA training in March 2024, but FSPCA certificates are typically valid for 3 years, so it should be current through March 2027, but I have not verified this. Low confidence in whether the weekly Listeria monitoring frequency is adequate without reviewing the actual environmental monitoring history and trend data; the plan does not justify this frequency, and more information would be needed to confirm it is appropriate for a 45-day shelf-life product. Cannot assess whether the company is actually following these procedures without reviewing the actual monitoring logs and corrective action records.

WILLAMETTE VALLEY FOODS, INC.
FOOD SAFETY PLAN
Ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips
Salem Plant, 1850 Fairgrounds Road NE, Salem, Oregon 97301
Effective date: May 12, 2025
Prepared by: Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager, Preventive Controls Qualified Individual
(PCQI certificate, FSPCA course, March 2024)
Approved by: Plant Manager
1. Facility and product description
Willamette Valley Foods produces refrigerated ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips in 8-ounce and 16-
ounce sealed plastic tubs for retail sale in Oregon, Washington and Idaho. The Salem plant operates one
shift, five days a week, with 28 production employees. Products are made from cooked chickpeas or black
beans, tahini, lemon juice, garlic, olive oil, salt and spices, blended, filled, sealed, coded and held
refrigerated at or below 41°F. Shelf life is 45 days refrigerated. Products are labeled with the allergen
statement "Contains: sesame" for all hummus items.
2. Process flow
Receiving of dry beans, tahini and other ingredients → dry storage or refrigerated storage → soaking and
cooking of beans (kettle, 212°F, 60 minutes minimum) → cooling in the blast chiller → blending with
other ingredients → filling and sealing → date coding → metal detection → refrigerated storage →
shipping.

ferrous, 3.0 mm stainless test pieces
5. Monitoring
The kettle operator records the internal temperature and the time at the start and end of each cook batch
on the cook log. The blast chiller operator records the temperature at 2 hours and at 6 hours on the cooling
log. The sanitation lead records the ATP swab result before each start-up. The line lead runs the three
metal test pieces through the detector at start-up, every two hours, and at the end of the run, and records
the result. The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs
the label log.
6. Corrective actions
If a cook batch does not reach 212°F for 60 minutes, the batch is re-cooked to the critical limit or
discarded, and the cause is recorded. If cooling exceeds the time limits, the batch is discarded. If an ATP
swab fails, the surface is re-cleaned and re-swabbed before production starts. If a Listeria spp. swab is
positive, the site is cleaned and re-swabbed, adjacent sites are added, and product made on that line since
the last negative swab is held pending investigation. If the metal detector fails a test piece, all product
since the last passing test is re-run through the detector. If a label does not match the formulation, the lot
is quarantined and not used. All corrective actions are recorded on the corrective action log and reviewed
by the PCQI within seven days.
7. Verification
The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven
working days of their creation. Probe thermometers are calibrated in ice water and boiling water weekly,
and the metal detector is serviced by the manufacturer annually. Finished product is tested for Listeria
monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory. Environmental monitoring results are trended
quarterly.
8. Supply-chain program
Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit
certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot. The approved supplier list is maintained by the quality
manager.
9. Records
All records named in this plan are kept at the Salem plant for at least two years from the date of the record
and are available to FDA and the Oregon Department of Agriculture on request. Records are reviewed and
signed by the PCQI as described in section 7.
10. Training
All production employees receive food hygiene training at hire and annually. The PCQI holds a current
FSPCA certificate. Sanitation and line leads are trained on the monitoring procedures in this plan.
